scenes.title: Cold open
narration: Every June 12th, Lisbon's rival districts transform the Avenida da Liberdade into a sea of handmade costumes and 'manjerico' plants to compete for the city's most prestigious title.
This is Marchas Populares. 20th century to present.

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Historical records mention neighborhood marches in Lisbon as early as the 18th century, but the competitive tradition began in 1932.
Organized by José Leitão de Barros and Norberto de Araújo, the first event aimed to centralize the various local celebrations into a single grand parade.
By 1940, the marches took on national significance during the double centenary of the Portuguese State and the Restoration of Independence.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The marches take place on the eve of Saint Anthony's Day (June 12th) as part of the Midsummer celebrations.
They represent neighborhood identity and rivalry.
The event is also a celebration of the 'Santos Populares' (Popular Saints).

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance is performed as a choreographed march-parade.
Participants move in synchronized formations, often utilizing the space of a wide avenue or arena.
The movement style is categorized as a quadrille, involving geometric patterns, turns, and rhythmic walking steps.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Costumes are handmade and elaborate, designed to reflect the year's specific theme while incorporating traditional Portuguese motifs.
Common visual elements include the 'manjerico' plant and maritime symbols.
The primary setting is the Avenida da Liberdade in Lisbon, which is lined with spectators, though preliminary judging occurs in closed stadiums like the Altice Arena.

scenes.title: The people
narration: José Leitão de Barros is credited with creating the modern competitive format in 1932.
Amália Rodrigues, the famous Fado singer, was a notable participant in the Marcha de Alcântara.
While the Lisbon competition is the most famous, similar 'Marchas Populares' are held in other Portuguese towns and villages, such as Setúbal.
The dance is a folk-derived quadrille that evolved from 18th-century neighborhood 'arraiais' (street parties) into a structured, televised competition.

music_brief.prompt: Original instrumental composition in the musical world of Marchas Populares (Portugal). New melody, new arrangement: do not quote or imitate any specific recorded song; keep the idiom, the instruments, the pulse and the proportions.

tracks.use: chapters: dance it to the music

rules: Original composition only — no sampling, no melody of any existing recording, no lyrics from any song.
Traditional public-domain tunes may be used only when the profile names them and a public-domain source is on file; otherwise compose new material in the idiom.
Keep the proportions true: the meter, the tempo range and the instrument roles the sources describe.
Label every generated track with the tool, the date and this brief, so provenance is always clear.

visual_brief.costume_notes: Costumes are handmade and elaborate, designed to reflect the year's specific theme while incorporating traditional Portuguese motifs. Common visual elements include the 'manjerico' plant and maritime symbols. The primary setting is the Avenida da Liberdade in Lisbon, which is lined with spectators, though preliminary judging occurs in closed stadiums like the Altice Arena.
visual_brief.setting_notes: The marches take place on the eve of Saint Anthony's Day (June 12th) as part of the Midsummer celebrations. They represent neighborhood identity and rivalry. The event is also a celebration of the 'Santos Populares' (Popular Saints). It is a night of communal feasting, where spectators eat grilled sardines and drink beer while watching the parade.
